title: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails
description_short: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails
description_medium: A Senate investigative committee later found that Roger Stone told Donald Trump and campaign officials to expect a WikiLeaks release from Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta’s account. The committee could not establish how much of Stone’s information was authentic or nonpublic. Its report also described Stone’s coordination with Jerome Corsi over an explanation for the information and the deletion of related communications.
description_long: The timeline reports that Roger Stone learned in early August 2016 that WikiLeaks planned to release emails from John Podesta, then chairman of Hillary Clinton’s campaign, and relayed that expectation to Donald Trump and campaign officials. The Senate Intelligence Committee later confirmed that the information was shared with Trump, Paul Manafort, Rick Gates, and likely others. It could not reliably determine how much authentic, nonpublic knowledge Stone had about WikiLeaks or the source of that knowledge. Jerome Corsi, whom Stone was believed to have relied on, gave contradictory accounts of whether he had received a tip or inferred the target himself. The committee also described Corsi and Stone coordinating a cover story and Corsi deleting communications. On October 7, Stone asked WikiLeaks to release the emails as a distraction from the Access Hollywood recording. The record documents advance knowledge and communications; it does not resolve precisely what Trump or campaign officials knew about the source or timing.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails

notes: Uses the supplied synopsis and linked timeline page. The Senate report is quoted there; uncertainty about the source and extent of advance knowledge is retained.

title: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views
description_short: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views
description_medium: A Center for Countering Digital Hate report estimated that Elon Musk’s political posts on X received 17.1 billion views after he endorsed Donald Trump on July 13, 2024, through the run-up to the election. The report said that total was more than twice the views recorded for political campaign ads in X’s disclosure dataset over the same period. The figure describes reported views, not a demonstrated effect on voters.
description_long: The Center for Countering Digital Hate reported that Elon Musk’s political posts on X accumulated 17.1 billion views between his July 13, 2024 endorsement of Donald Trump and the election. The report characterized many of the posts as false or misleading and compared their reported reach with X’s own disclosure data for political campaign advertisements, which recorded less than half as many views during the same period. This entry records a measure of exposure on a platform owned by Musk during a presidential campaign; it does not establish how many distinct people saw the posts, whether viewers accepted them, or whether they changed votes. The linked timeline page also places the number in the context of Musk’s increased visibility on the platform after a 2023 effort to address the reach of his posts. Its comparison is about the report’s view counts, not a finding that organic posts and paid advertisements are identical. The main documented point is the scale the advocacy group attributed to Musk’s political posting before the 2024 election.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views

notes: Uses the report figures and comparison as attributed in the supplied linked timeline; distinguishes views from audience size or persuasive effect.

title: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama
description_short: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama
description_medium: On September 2, 2025, Donald Trump announced that he had chosen to move U.S. Space Command’s headquarters from Colorado to Alabama. Colorado’s congressional delegation criticized the decision, citing readiness, expense, and strategic concerns. Trump also attacked Colorado’s mail-voting system. The timeline interprets the relocation as political retaliation, while reporting both the stated cost concerns and an inspector general warning about readiness risks.
description_long: Donald Trump announced on September 2, 2025, that U.S. Space Command headquarters would move from Colorado to Alabama. Colorado’s entire congressional delegation criticized the decision, arguing that relocation could delay space-defense readiness, waste public money, and benefit strategic rivals; four members of the delegation were Republicans. Trump separately criticized Colorado’s election rules, falsely describing the state’s mail-voting system as automatically crooked, although voters can also vote in person. The timeline presents the relocation as punishment for Colorado’s voting record and reward for Alabama’s support, while noting that Trump denied that political support explained his choice. The practical costs described in the report are substantial: moving the headquarters could take three to four years, cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and require about 1,700 personnel to relocate. A Pentagon inspector general had warned of readiness risks. The report also notes an estimated $426 million long-term cost advantage for Huntsville, which would take time to realize. These competing claims and costs are part of the record; the announcement itself does not settle the strategic or financial case for the move.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama

notes: Uses the supplied linked timeline page. Political-retaliation language is attributed to the timeline’s interpretation; the reported cost and readiness claims are presented with attribution.

title: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein
description_short: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein
description_medium: The timeline says Les Wexner transferred ownership of his Manhattan townhouse at 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein in 1995 or earlier; the exact date is unknown. The transfer became public in a January 1996 New York Times story. Wexner had bought the seven-story house in 1989 for $13.2 million and spent tens of millions on renovations and furnishings. Epstein later confirmed that the house was his.
description_long: This entry concerns a property transfer between Les Wexner and Jeffrey Epstein. The timeline dates it to 1995 or earlier but says the precise date is unknown; it became public through a New York Times story in January 1996. Wexner had purchased the seven-story Manhattan townhouse at 9 East 71st Street in 1989 for $13.2 million and invested tens of millions more in renovations, art, and furnishings. The newspaper described Epstein as Wexner’s protégé and one of his financial advisers. When asked about the property, Epstein said that it was now his and that Wexner had rarely stayed there. The account also described unusual luxury features, including a concealed, reinforced bathroom and a heated sidewalk, illustrating the scale of the residence rather than establishing anything about the transfer’s legal terms. The supplied material documents a significant asset given by Wexner to Epstein and the financial relationship the newspaper described. It does not establish a role for Donald Trump in this transfer, despite the record’s broader Trump-related framing.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein

notes: The exact transfer date is uncertain in the source. The TrumpFile timeline quotes the linked 1996 New York Times story; no connection between Trump and this transfer is asserted.

title: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020
description_short: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020
description_medium: On September 7, 2020, Jack Posobiec posted about “Stop The Steal 2020” while Ali Alexander told a Periscope audience he was building a digital campaign under that slogan. Alexander described a database and alert system for Trump supporters near election offices, vote-counting sites, and related court proceedings. The timeline says pro-Trump Facebook pages began using the phrase hours later, while leaving their authorship uncertain.
description_long: The timeline records two same-day developments on September 7, 2020. Jack Posobiec, described as a far-right social-media personality and One America News correspondent, tweeted about “Stop The Steal 2020.” Ali Alexander separately told viewers on Periscope that he was building a digital campaign to “stop the steal.” Alexander said the effort would compile a database of Trump supporters and map locations in swing states where ballots were counted or election officials worked. He described collecting cellphone numbers so people within 100 miles could be alerted to places he characterized as improper vote counting or to federal court hearings. He later released a website and app for building that database. The timeline reports that pro-Trump Facebook pages began using the phrase “Stop The Steal” within hours, but says those pages may have been run by Alexander, Posobiec, or others. The account documents campaign planning and stated intentions; it does not show from this entry alone how many people joined, whether alerts were sent, or what actions followed at election offices.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020

notes: Uses the linked timeline and preserves its uncertainty about who operated the Facebook pages; distinguishes stated plans from completed activity.

title: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe
description_short: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe
description_medium: A March 2025 account of a private Signal conversation quotes White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller saying Donald Trump had approved strikes on the Houthis and that the United States should seek economic returns from Europe and Egypt. Miller discussed what to do if Europe did not contribute. The message frames military action as leverage; it does not establish that the proposed economic terms were implemented.
description_long: The timeline describes a private Signal conversation on March 14, 2025, in which White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller discussed U.S. strikes on Yemen’s Houthi movement with administration officials. Miller wrote that Trump had given a “green light” and argued that the United States should make clear what it expected from Egypt and Europe in return. He raised the question of how to enforce a requirement if Europe did not pay, describing a need for further economic gain after restoring freedom of navigation. The timeline notes that Signal was not authorized for confidential government communications. It places the message against Houthi attacks on U.S. and U.K.-linked shipping in the Red Sea and the resulting diversion of commercial and military traffic to longer routes. The proposal, as quoted, treats military action as a way to obtain political or economic leverage from countries that would benefit from safer passage. The account does not show that a payment arrangement or such enforcement mechanism was adopted. Its significance lies in the stated rationale and the use of a private messaging channel for policy discussion.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe

notes: Quotes the private message as reproduced by the linked timeline. The economic leverage proposal is described as discussion, not as an implemented policy.

title: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge
description_short: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge
description_medium: In March 2017, the Trump administration demanded the immediate resignation of all 46 U.S. attorneys appointed under Barack Obama. Preet Bharara, whom Trump had asked to remain, was among those dismissed after refusing to leave. The mass request came while investigations and prosecutions were underway. The supplied synopsis contrasts the abrupt removals with the gradual transitions legal experts described as customary and notes concerns about political influence over prosecutorial appointments.
description_long: On March 10, 2017, the Trump administration demanded the immediate resignation of all 46 U.S. attorneys appointed during the Obama administration. Preet Bharara was among them; according to the supplied synopsis, Trump had personally asked him to stay, and Bharara had refused a White House phone call before the dismissal. The timing drew attention because federal investigations and prosecutions were ongoing. The synopsis says legal experts described gradual replacement of U.S. attorneys as the usual way for a new administration to preserve continuity in federal law enforcement. It also connects concern about political motivation to Bharara’s investigations involving Trump allies and associates. Those points are presented as the record’s account and interpretation, not as a judicial finding about the administration’s motive. The episode became an early test of the boundary between a president’s authority to appoint prosecutors and the expectation that law-enforcement decisions remain independent of personal or partisan interests. The source is a contemporaneous New York Times report; the entry focuses on the broad, immediate demand and its implications for continuity and public confidence.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge

notes: Uses the detailed supplied synopsis because the linked New York Times page returned HTTP 403 in this sandbox. Motive is attributed to the synopsis and not presented as a legal finding.

title: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister
description_short: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister
description_medium: In an interview at Jeffrey Epstein’s New York mansion, journalist James B. Stewart asked about rumors that Epstein was helping Tesla find a chairman after a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation. Epstein claimed he had been working with Elon Musk and Tesla and said he was discussing investment with Saudi Arabia. Musk and Tesla denied contact. The account leaves Epstein’s claim unconfirmed and notes Stewart’s uncertainty about later dinner invitations.
description_long: The linked account describes a 2018 interview in which New York Times journalist James B. Stewart visited Jeffrey Epstein at his Manhattan home. Epstein claimed that he had been working with Elon Musk and Tesla, amid rumors that he was helping the company find a new chairman after an SEC investigation. Epstein told Stewart that Tesla would not confirm their contact because he was “radioactive,” and said he was speaking with Saudi Arabia about investment. Musk and Tesla denied ever contacting Epstein; the account does not independently establish Epstein’s claim. Epstein also discussed the possibility of becoming a minister, saying that people might use him as a confidant, and made comments minimizing the criminality of sex with underage girls. Those remarks are part of Stewart’s reported interview and illustrate the way Epstein described his relationships and conduct; they should not be treated as proof that the claimed business work occurred. Stewart later received dinner invitations involving Epstein and public figures, but said he could not confirm whether the dinners took place. The event is principally a record of Epstein’s claims and the denials that followed.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister

notes: Uses the linked timeline page and distinguishes Epstein’s claim from the denials by Musk and Tesla. Dinner invitations are not presented as confirmed events.

title: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack
description_short: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack
description_medium: On March 25, 2021, seven House committees requested records from 16 federal agencies as part of a review of the Trump administration’s handling of the January 6 Capitol attack and decisions leading up to it. The requests reached agencies including the White House, Justice Department, FBI, Pentagon, and National Guard. The inquiry followed the failure to secure bipartisan agreement on an independent commission; it sought information and did not itself establish findings.
description_long: Seven House committees opened a broad records inquiry on March 25, 2021, sending letters to 16 federal agencies for communications about January 6 and the federal government’s preparations and response. The review examined decisions dating back to December 1 and the Trump administration’s handling of the attack on the Capitol. Requests went to the White House, National Archives, Justice Department, FBI, Pentagon, National Guard, Homeland Security, Interior Department, U.S. Park Police, and intelligence community, as well as congressional security offices and Washington, D.C. authorities. The effort came after Speaker Nancy Pelosi had been unable to secure bipartisan cooperation for an independent commission. At the time described by the linked account, federal prosecutors had charged more than 300 people in connection with breaching the Capitol, including people accused of conspiring to stop Electoral College certification. The committees’ letters were an investigative step: asking agencies to preserve and provide records did not amount to a completed inquiry or a finding about the administration’s responsibility. The entry documents the scope of the information request and the institutional effort to reconstruct decisions before and during the attack.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack

notes: Uses the linked timeline page for the committee requests. Describes the letters as an investigative step, not a completed finding.

title: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies
description_short: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued orders halting new offshore wind leasing in federal waters and directing agencies to review existing leases, while also seeking to claw back clean-energy subsidies authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act. The supplied synopsis says projects and jobs faced disruption and that states and companies challenged the actions, including on contract grounds. The record describes the policy direction and ensuing legal disputes, not their final outcomes.
description_long: The supplied synopsis says that on January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued executive orders stopping new offshore wind leasing in federal waters and directing agencies to review whether existing leases should be terminated. It also describes an effort to claw back clean-energy subsidies authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act. The orders affected an industry whose projects and investment plans depended on federal lease agreements; the synopsis says the halt threatened projects and tens of thousands of jobs. Companies and states challenged the actions, arguing that retroactively ending leases or related arrangements could violate contractual commitments. Those lawsuits show that the orders raised disputes over the government’s obligations, but the supplied record does not report a final court resolution. The policy represented a move away from federal support for offshore wind and certain clean-energy incentives. This description distinguishes the directives and reviews described in the entry from completed cancellations: the source summary says agencies were directed to review existing leases, not that every lease was immediately terminated. The linked Federal Register item is the official order identified in the record; the additional consequences and litigation are drawn from the supplied synopsis.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies

notes: Uses the detailed supplied synopsis; the linked Federal Register page blocked automated access. Describes reviews and litigation without claiming a final court outcome.
